latin.1952: THESIS I. SOCINUS & ejus asseclae intelligere non valentes, qua ratione certo praescire possint futura contingentia, & quae non habent causam necessariam & determinatam, ejusmodi futurorum certam praescientiam in ipso Deo dari negant.
latin.1953: II. Sed mirum est homines divinam authoritatem Scripturae tribuentes, hoc in animum inducere posse. Nihil enim evidentius ex Scriptura colligitur, quam Deum futura quaelibet praenosse, quod manifestum faciunt quae in Scripturis habentur Prophetarum praedictiones. Nam ut scite Tertullianus, Praescientia Dei tot habet testes, quot Deus fecit Prophetas. Neque enim Prophetae potuerunt, inspirante Deo, ea praedicere quae post multa demum secula contigerunt, & ab hominibus libere sunt facta, nisi quae talia sunt ab aeterno Deo nota sunt.
latin.1954: III. Porro Deum multa praedixisse pluribus post seculis ab hominibus libere agenda, innumeris exemplis ex Scriptura probari potest. Sic decimo quinto capite Geneseos, Praedixit Deus Aegyptios afflicturos semen Abrahami quadringentis annis, & eos, populum illum sic affligendo, graviter peccaturos esse, & iram Dei in se provocaturos. Scito, inquit Deus Abrahamo, quod peregrinum futurum sit semen tuum in terra non sua: & subjicient eos servituti, & affligent quadringentis annis. Veruntamen gentem cui servituri sunt ego judicabo.
latin.1955: IV. Sic quoque Deuteronomii capite trigesimo primo Deus ad Mosen dixisse legitur, Ecce tu dormiturus es cum Patribus tuis: postea surget populus iste, & fornicabitur post Deos alienigenas terrae, ad quam pergit ut habitet in medio ejus; & derelinquet me, irritumque faciet pactum meum, quod pepigi cum eo. Quas praedictiones certas & infallibiles fuisse, eventus docuit illis per omnia respondens.
latin.1956: V. Similiter apud Prophetas multis in locis praedicta est incredulitas Judaeorum futura tempore Messiae, & propter eam istius populi futura quoque rejectio. Praesertim apud Isaiam capite quinquagesimo tertio. Quis credidit auditui nostro, & brachium Domini cui est revelatum? Et ibidem haec incredulitas tanta futura esse praedicitur, ut Regem suum Messiam despectui sint habituri, quin & vulneraturi, acerbissimaque & ignominiosissima morte e medio sublaturi, praevaricatoribusque & sceleratis adnumeraturi. Et Messias ipse Jesus Dominus noster, quum in terris versaretur, omnia ista quae primores gentis Judaicae in ipsum admissuri erant, scelera & flagitia sigillatim praedixit, addens oportere ista omnia sic fieri, & sic perficienda omnia quae scripta sunt per Prophetas de filio hominis.
latin.1957: VI. Insignis est praesertim praedictio Christi de Juda, quod ipsum proditurus esset, idque multo antequam Satan immisisset istud in cor ejus. Imo pluribus ante Christi adventum seculis, eandem proditionem praedixerat Deus per Prophetas. Huc enim testatur Christus spectare verba Davidis Psalmo quadragesimo primo, Qui manducat mecum panem, levavit contra me calcaneum suum, Joan. 13. Et Petrus respiciens ad ea quae leguntur Psalmo centesimo nono dicit, Oportuisse impleri scripturam hanc, quam praedixit Spiritus Sanctus per os Davidis, de Juda, &c. Act. 1.
latin.1958: VII. His addi possunt quae leguntur apud Danielem praedicta de Antiochi Epiphanis impietate, superbia, libidine, & saevitia, qua in Judaeos grassaturus erat, & ipsum Dei templum profanaturus. Itemque apud Paulum de adventu filii illius perditionis qui in templo Dei sessurus, & supra ipsum Deum se elaturus erat, plurimosque in errorem mendacibus signis inducturus. Quae omnia cum ab hominibus libere patranda fuerint, a Dei spiritu in scripturis loquente, certo, clare, & sigillatim, uti factum videmus, praedici non potuerunt, nisi Deus omnium futurorum eventuum, quantumlibet contingentium, certam & distinctam notitiam habeat.
latin.1959: VIII. Et certe si Deus ab aeterno futura quaelibet non praescit, sed ignorat ea quae sunt a creaturis libere agenda, omniscientia Deo amplius tribuenda non est; neque vere dici potest omnia scire, siquidem nonnulla sunt quae latent ejus scientiam.
latin.1960: IX. Inde sequetur etiam Deum non esse omnis mutationis expertem. Cum enim Deus praesentia cognoscat, si antequam essent illa ignorabat, aliquid didicit ipso rerum eventu, & factus est ex non sciente sciens, quod sine aliqua in Deo mutatione concipi non potest. Quin inde consequens est, scientiam Dei perfectam non esse, quandoquidem, ex hac hypothesi, quotidie in cognitione augetur & proficit.
latin.1961: X. Neque contra tam apertam veritatem ullam vim habent quae objicere solent Sociniani. Quale est, Scripturam Deum inducere propter hominum peccata tristitia affectum, & poenitentia ductum. Videns, inquit illa, Dominus quod multa malitia hominum esset in terra, & cuncta cognitio cordis intenta esset ad malum omni tempore, poenituit eum quod hominem fecisset in terra: Et tactus dolore cordis intrinsecus, Delebo, inquit, hominem quem creavi a facie terrae, Geneseos capite sexto. Unde colligunt Deum, antequam sic homines ruerent in omne scelus, non pro certo novisse tantam eorum fore malitiam; Nam alioqui videtur absque ratione dici, illa visa, dolore tactus, & poenitentia affectus fuisse quod hominem creasset. Neque enim aliquis poenitentia ducitur ob ea quae fecerit, nisi nova quaedam ipsum cognitio subeat, aut contingat quiddam ipsi inexpectatum, & non ante praevisum.
latin.1962: XI. Et certe Deum quiddam circa liberas hominum actiones de novo discere, plane confici videtur ipsius Dei verbis Abrahamum alloquentis, ejusdem libri capite vigesimo secundo. Postquam enim Abraham se paratum ostendisset ad filium, ex Dei mandato, immolandum; Nunc cognovi, inquit Dominus, quod timeas Deum, quia non pepercisti unigenito tuo filio propter me.
latin.1963: XII. Imo Scriptura docere videtur quaedam aliter contingere quam Deus ipse conjecerit, quandoquidem affirmat quaedam ab hominibus fieri, contra quam ipse expectarat. Ut quum Deus ita de contumacia & rebellione populi Judaici queritur, Quid est quod debui ultra facere vineae meae, & non feci ei? Cur expectavi ut faceret uvas, & fecit labruscas? apud Isaiam cap. quinto.
latin.1964: XIII. Verum ad ista dicendum est, scripturam saepe Deo tribuere hominum membra & affectus tropice atque figurate, non autem quod ad litteram & proprie ipsi conveniant: ac proinde multa quae de Deo dicuntur ἀνθρωποπαθῶς, intelligenda esse θεοπρεπῶς, & modo qui Deo dignus sit. Itaque quum scriptura dicit, Deum fuisse poenitentia ductum, nihilo magis necesse est ut istud proprie sumamus, quam quod alibi legitur viscera Dei commota fuisse, & in nares ejus ascendisse fumum. Imo quum poenitentiam scriptura proprie sumit, expresse illam a Deo removet. Ut quum Samuel dicit ad Saulem, Triumphator, sive fortitudo, Israelis non mentietur, & poenitudine non flectetur: neque enim homo est ut agat poenitentiam, 1 Sam. 15. Poenitentia igitur in Deo significat non affectum, sed effectum. Ac quum ait scriptura Deum poenituisse, antecedens pro consequente sumit, & significat Deum illud fecisse, quod faceret homo quem poenitet operis a se facti: nempe statuisse Deum homines a se factos, de terra, propter ipsorum iniquitatem delere; sicut homo destruit opus cujus ipsum poenitet.
latin.1965: XIV. Eodem modo Deus propter hominum peccata contristari dicitur, non quod in se sentiat affectum aliquem nostrae tristitiae similem; sed simpliciter ad significandum hominum peccata Deo multum improbari atque displicere, & talia esse quae Deo tristitiam afferrent, si nostri similis esset, atque ὁμοιοπαθής: ita ut hic consequens pro antecedente sumatur, tristitia, scilicet, pro eo quod in subjecto capaci tristitiam gignere aptum est.
latin.1966: XV. Similiter apud Isaiam, Dominus a vinea sua dicitur expectasse uvas cum illa fecerit labruscas; non quod Deus anceps & dubius esset de eo quod faceret populus Judaicus, vinea ista figuratus, post tot adhibita media ad illum ad veram pietatem formandum; sed quoniam ea fecerat quae plane populum istum in rectam viam reducere debebant, & quae, si homo erga hominem adhibuisset, legitime sperare & expectare posset cor ejus inde emolliendum esse, & flectendum ad amorem & ultroneum obsequium.
latin.1967: XVI. Quum autem Deus dicit ad Abrahamum, Nunc cognovi quod timeas Deum, quia non pepercisti unigenito tuo filio propter me. Significare non vult se prius de Abrahami pietate dubitasse, neque Abrahamum ipsi fuisse satis cognitum; sed tantum Abrahamum, dum paratus fuit proprium filium, Deo jubente, immolare, sui erga Deum amoris & timoris, certum & indubitatum experimentum dedisse, & tale quo posset convinci, qui ea de re hactenus dubitasset, neque fuisset satis certus & persuasus.
latin.1968: XVII. Neque majorem vim habet argumentum quod petunt illi quos impugnamus, ex libri Numerorum capite 14. Ubi dicitur Deus jurasse se introducturum populum suum in terram Canaan; & tamen propter ipsorum peccatum atque incredulitatem rursus jurat se non amplius id facturum. Vivo ego, ait Dominus, sicut loquuti estis audiente me, sic faciam vobis. In solitudine hac jacebunt cadavera vestra. Omnes qui numerati estis a viginti annis & supra, & murmurastis contra me, non intrabitis terram super quam levavi manum meam, ut habitare vos facerem, praeter Caleb filium Jephune, & Josue filium Nun. Quis enim, inquiunt, ex ipsis hominibus ita amens est, ut ex animo juret se aliquid facturum, quod se facturum minime esse jam probe novit, seu causas, cur id nullo modo facturus sit, jam exploratissimas habeat? Aut quid Deo indignius, quam se aliquid facturum jurare, non animo, sed verbis tantum?
latin.1969: XVIII. Sed verum est quidem Deum saepius juravisse se daturum posteris Abrahami terram Canaan, & ad illa juramenta multis in locis memorata respiciunt verba quae modo citavimus. Juramentum autem istud speciatim spectavisse illos ex Israelitis qui in deserto fuerunt rebelles, non probatur ex verbis citatis, Non intrabitis terram super quam levavi manum meam, ut habitare VOS facerem. Nam ibi particula Vos indefinite designat gentem Israeliticam, non vero singulariter personas quae tum illam constituebant. Neque tamen in eo quicquam esset absurdi, si diceremus Deum speciatim hominibus illis ingressum in terram Canaan cum juramento promisisse, non absolute, sed sub conditione, quanquam praevideret conditionem illam ab iis non esse implendam; modo conditio ista pertinuerit ad eorum officium, & talis fuerit quam possent & deberent implere. Neque inter ipsos homines amens esset, qui juraret alicui se hoc aut illud facturum, modo in viri boni officio perstaret, quanquam haberet pro certo fore ut alter ille officio suo minime fungeretur.
latin.1970: XIX. Sed qui hodie contendunt in Deo non esse certam praescientiam futurorum contingentium, eo praecipue moventur quod, si ea quae libere homines facturi sunt Deus certo praevidet, & quidem ab aeterno, non potest, ut ipsi existimant, homines serio monere, hortari, atque obtestari, ut convertantur atq; resipiscant. Ad quid enim opus est sollicite aliquem hortari atque compellere, ut faciat id quod pro comperto habes illum esse facturum; aut cui bono uti sollicitatione, & obtestatione multa, apud eum quem exploratum tibi est nihil eorum quae rogas facturum esse?
latin.1971: XX. Sed tantum abest ut praevisa hominum contumacia, vel obedientia obstet quominus Deus serio illos monere, rogare, & hortari possit: ut contra Deus illam non possit praevidere, quin prius praevideat, & apud se constituat se ita serio cum hominibus acturum. Nam divinae monitiones, hortationes, & obtestationes sunt media quibus procuratur hominum obedientia; & praesupposita quaedam, sine quibus Deo rebelles, & in ipsum contumaces esse & dici non possunt.
latin.1972: XXI. Caeterum non dedecere sapientiam divinam, ut illos quos Deus certo scit monitis, hortatibus, & praeceptis ipsius nequaquam obtemperaturos, nihilominus compellat, hortetur & invitet modis omnibus ad resipiscentiam, convinci possunt illi ipsi quibus cum nobis res est. Fatentur enim quosdam, divino judicio pertinacem eorum malitiam ulciscente, sic excaecatos & induratos esse, ut resipiscere nequeant. Et tamen negare non possunt Deum erga illos ipsos quos optime novit sic affectos & dispositos esse, uti monitionibus, & obtestationibus quibus homines solet ad officium compellere, ut vel ex solo Pharaonis exemplo manifestum est. Si ergo in his, aut circa hos, fatentibus adversariis, locum habere possunt seriae Dei obtestationes, comminationes, querelae, sine ulla justitiae Dei violatione, aut sapientiae imminutione, cur idem in caeteris, quos Deus ab aeterno, ex libero voluntatis & mentis proposito, novit non obsequuturos, locum habere non valeat?
latin.1973: XXII. Vana sunt ergo quaecunque ex scripturis proferuntur adversus aeternam Dei praescientiam, qua certo & distincte novit quaecunque sunt a creaturis tempore quovis libere agenda. Sequitur jam ut videamus quomodo creaturarum libertas in agendo cum aeterna ista Dei praescientia stare possit. Non parum enim hic est difficultatis quae pridem ingenia Doctorum exercuit. Nam cum impossibile sit Dei praescientiam falli, fieri non potest quin eveniant ea quae Deus eventura praevidit; adeoque omnia necessario eveniunt, & impossibile est quin ipsa hominum voluntas eos producat & eliciat actus, quos ab ea producendos Deus ab aeterno praenoscit: & sic videtur prorsus perire actionum humanarum libertas. Etenim qua ratione liberum dici poterit, quod impossibile est non fieri, aut aliter fieri?

sections.title: Socinus and his followers deny that God has certain foreknowledge of future contingents
sections.pass_a: THESIS I. SOCINUS and his followers not being able to understand, by what reason future contingents can be certainly foreknown, and things which have not a necessary and determinate cause, deny that a certain foreknowledge of futures of this kind is given in God himself.
pass_b: Socinus and his followers cannot understand how future contingents, things that have no necessary and determinate cause, can be known in advance with certainty.
They therefore deny that God himself has any certain foreknowledge of future events of this kind.

choices.why: The Schools' term for future events without a necessary and determinate cause; kept as a technical term.

sections.title: Scripture plainly teaches God's foreknowledge: the prophets are its witnesses (Tertullian)
sections.pass_a: But it is wonderful that men attributing divine authority to Scripture, can bring their mind to this. For nothing is more evidently gathered from Scripture, than that God foreknew any future things whatever, which the predictions of the Prophets that are had in the Scriptures make manifest. For as Tertullian aptly says, The foreknowledge of God has as many witnesses, as God has made Prophets. For neither could the Prophets, God inspiring them, foretell those things which at length happened after many ages, and were done freely by men, unless such things were known to God from eternity.
pass_b: It is astonishing that people who grant Scripture divine authority can persuade themselves of this. Nothing is gathered more plainly from Scripture than that God knew beforehand every future thing, as the prophecies recorded in it make clear.

As Tertullian neatly puts it, 'God's foreknowledge has as many witnesses as God has made prophets.' The prophets, inspired by God, could not have foretold things that happened only many ages later and were done freely by human beings unless those things were known to God from eternity.

lemmas.latin: Praescientia Dei tot habet testes, quot Deus fecit Prophetas
lemmas.gloss: The foreknowledge of God has as many witnesses, as God has made Prophets

choices.why: The standard English term for God's knowing in advance; 'foreknowledge' is kept throughout for praescientia, with 'foresee' for praevidere.

notes: The Tertullian saying is from Adversus Marcionem, book 2, chapter 5.

sections.title: God foretold free acts centuries ahead: the oppression in Egypt (Genesis 15)
sections.pass_a: Further that God foretold many things to be done freely by men many ages after, can be proved from Scripture by innumerable examples. Thus in the fifteenth chapter of Genesis, God foretold that the Egyptians would afflict the seed of Abraham four hundred years, and that they, by so afflicting that people, would sin grievously, and provoke the wrath of God upon themselves. Know, says God to Abraham, that thy seed shall be a stranger in a land not their own: and they shall bring them into servitude, and afflict them four hundred years. But the nation whom they shall serve I will judge.
pass_b: Countless examples from Scripture prove that God foretold many things that human beings would freely do many ages later.

In Genesis 15 God foretold that the Egyptians would oppress Abraham's descendants for four hundred years, and that in oppressing that people they would sin gravely and bring God's wrath on themselves. 'Know for certain,' God says to Abraham, 'that your descendants will be strangers in a land that is not theirs; they will be enslaved and oppressed for four hundred years. But I will judge the nation they serve.'

lemmas.gloss: provoke the wrath of God upon themselves

choices.why: The standard English term for God's knowing in advance; 'foreknowledge' is kept throughout for praescientia, with 'foresee' for praevidere.

sections.title: Deuteronomy 31: Israel's future idolatry foretold to Moses
sections.pass_a: Thus also in the thirty-first chapter of Deuteronomy God is read to have said to Moses, Behold thou shalt sleep with thy Fathers: afterward this people shall rise up, and go a whoring after the strange Gods of the land, whither it goes to dwell in the midst of it; and shall forsake me, and make void my covenant, which I made with it. Which predictions the event taught were certain and infallible, answering them in all things.
pass_b: Likewise in Deuteronomy 31 God is recorded as saying to Moses: 'You are about to sleep with your fathers. Then this people will rise up and prostitute themselves to the foreign gods of the land they are entering to live in. They will forsake me and break my covenant that I made with them.'
The outcome, matching these predictions in every respect, showed that they were certain and infallible.

choices.why: The standard English term for God's knowing in advance; 'foreknowledge' is kept throughout for praescientia, with 'foresee' for praevidere.

sections.title: The Jews' unbelief and the rejection of the Messiah foretold (Isaiah 53) and Christ's own predictions
sections.pass_a: Similarly among the Prophets in many places the unbelief of the Jews to come in the time of the Messiah was foretold, and on account of it the future rejection also of that people. Especially in Isaiah in the fifty-third chapter. Who hath believed our report, and to whom is the arm of the Lord revealed? And in the same place this unbelief is foretold to be going to be so great, that they would hold their King the Messiah in contempt, nay and wound him, and take him away from the midst by a most bitter and most ignominious death, and number him with transgressors and wicked men. And the Messiah himself Jesus our Lord, while he lived on earth, foretold one by one all those crimes and outrages which the chief men of the Jewish nation were going to commit against him, adding that all these things must so come to pass, and that so all things must be accomplished which are written by the Prophets of the son of man.
pass_b: In many places the prophets also foretold that the Jews would not believe in the time of the Messiah, and that this people would therefore be rejected. This is especially so in Isaiah 53: 'Who has believed our message, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?'

There the prophet foretells that their unbelief would go so far that they would despise their King, the Messiah, even wound him, remove him by a most cruel and shameful death, and count him among transgressors and criminals. And the Messiah himself, Jesus our Lord, while he lived on earth, foretold one by one all the crimes and outrages that the leaders of the Jewish nation would commit against him. He added that all this must happen so, and that everything written by the prophets about the Son of Man must be fulfilled in this way.

choices.why: The standard English term for God's knowing in advance; 'foreknowledge' is kept throughout for praescientia, with 'foresee' for praevidere.

sections.title: Judas's betrayal foretold by Christ and, ages before, by David (Psalms 41 and 109)
sections.pass_a: Notable especially is the prediction of Christ concerning Judas, that he would betray him, and that long before Satan had put that into his heart. Nay many ages before the coming of Christ, God had foretold the same betrayal by the Prophets. For Christ testifies that the words of David in the forty-first Psalm look to this, He that eateth bread with me, hath lifted up his heel against me, John 13. And Peter looking to those things which are read in the hundred and ninth Psalm says, This scripture must needs have been fulfilled, which the Holy Spirit foretold by the mouth of David, concerning Judas, etc. Acts 1.
pass_b: Christ's prediction about Judas, that he would betray him, is especially striking, and it came long before Satan had put that into Judas's heart. Indeed, many ages before Christ's coming God had foretold the same betrayal through the prophets.

Christ testifies that this is what David's words in Psalm 41 refer to: 'He who eats bread with me has lifted his heel against me' (John 13). And Peter, with an eye to what is written in Psalm 109, says: 'The scripture had to be fulfilled which the Holy Spirit spoke beforehand through the mouth of David concerning Judas,' and so on (Acts 1).

lemmas.latin: antequam Satan immisisset istud in cor ejus
lemmas.gloss: before Satan had put that into his heart
This scripture must needs have been fulfilled

sections.title: Antiochus Epiphanes (Daniel) and the man of sin (Paul): such predictions require certain knowledge of contingents
sections.pass_a: To these can be added what are read foretold in Daniel of the impiety, pride, lust, and cruelty of Antiochus Epiphanes, with which he was going to rage against the Jews, and profane the very temple of God. And likewise in Paul of the coming of that son of perdition who was going to sit in the temple of God, and exalt himself above God himself, and lead very many into error by lying signs. All which since they were to be done freely by men, could not be foretold by the spirit of God speaking in the scriptures, certainly, clearly, and one by one, as we see was done, unless God has a certain and distinct knowledge of all future events, however contingent.
pass_b: To these may be added what Daniel foretells of the impiety, pride, lust and cruelty of Antiochus Epiphanes, with which he would rage against the Jews and profane God's own temple. Paul likewise foretells the coming of the son of perdition, who would sit in God's temple, exalt himself above God himself, and lead very many astray by lying signs.

All these things were to be done freely by human beings. The Spirit of God, speaking in Scripture, could not have foretold them certainly, clearly and one by one, as we see was done, unless God has certain and distinct knowledge of all future events, however contingent they may be.

choices.why: The Schools' term for future events without a necessary and determinate cause; kept as a technical term.

sections.title: Without foreknowledge of free acts God would not be omniscient
sections.pass_a: And certainly if God does not foreknow from eternity any future things whatever, but is ignorant of those things which are to be done freely by creatures, omniscience is no longer to be attributed to God; nor can he truly be said to know all things, since there are some things which lie hidden from his knowledge.
pass_b: Certainly, if God does not know every future thing from eternity, but is ignorant of what creatures will freely do, omniscience can no longer be ascribed to him.
Nor can he truly be said to know all things, since some things would be hidden from his knowledge.

choices.why: The standard English term for God's knowing in advance; 'foreknowledge' is kept throughout for praescientia, with 'foresee' for praevidere.

sections.title: It would also make God mutable and his knowledge imperfect
sections.pass_a: Thence it will follow also that God is not free from all change. For since God knows present things, if before they were he was ignorant of them, he learned something by the very event of things, and was made from not knowing knowing, which cannot be conceived without some change in God. Nay thence it is consequent, that the knowledge of God is not perfect, since, on this hypothesis, it is daily increased and advances in cognition.
pass_b: It would also follow that God is not free from all change. Since God knows present things, if he was ignorant of them before they existed, he learned something from the outcome itself and passed from not knowing to knowing, which cannot be conceived without some change in God.
It further follows that God's knowledge is not perfect, since on this hypothesis it grows and advances in what it knows every day.

choices.why: The standard English term for God's knowing in advance; 'foreknowledge' is kept throughout for praescientia, with 'foresee' for praevidere.

sections.title: The Socinian objection: Scripture says God grieved and repented that he had made man (Genesis 6)
sections.pass_a: Nor against so open a truth have those things any force which the Socinians are wont to object. Such as is, that Scripture brings in God affected with sadness on account of the sins of men, and led by repentance. The Lord seeing, it says, that the wickedness of men was great in the earth, and all the thought of the heart was intent upon evil at all times, it repented him that he had made man on the earth: And touched with sorrow of heart inwardly, I will destroy, he says, man whom I have created from the face of the earth, Genesis chapter six. Whence they gather that God, before men so rushed into every crime, did not know for certain that their wickedness would be so great; For otherwise it seems to be said without reason, that, these things seen, he was touched with sorrow, and affected with repentance that he had created man. For neither is any one led by repentance on account of those things which he has done, unless some new knowledge come upon him, or something happen to him unexpected, and not foreseen before.
pass_b: Against so plain a truth the objections the Socinians usually raise have no force. One is that Scripture presents God as saddened by human sins and moved to repentance: 'The Lord saw that human wickedness was great on the earth and that every thought of the heart was set on evil all the time, and he repented that he had made man on the earth. Grieved to the heart, he said, I will wipe man, whom I created, from the face of the earth' (Genesis 6).

From this they infer that before human beings plunged into every kind of crime God did not know for certain that their wickedness would be so great. Otherwise, they say, there seems to be no reason for saying that on seeing it he was grieved and repented of having created man. No one repents of what he has done unless some new knowledge comes to him, or something happens to him that he did not expect and had not foreseen.

choices.why: The standard English term for God's knowing in advance; 'foreknowledge' is kept throughout for praescientia, with 'foresee' for praevidere.

sections.title: A second objection: 'Now I know that you fear God' (Genesis 22)
sections.pass_a: And certainly that God learns something anew about the free actions of men, seems plainly to be concluded from the words of God himself addressing Abraham, in the twenty-second chapter of the same book. For after Abraham had shown himself ready to sacrifice his son, by the command of God; Now I know, says the Lord, that thou fearest God, because thou hast not spared thine only begotten son for my sake.
pass_b: And certainly it seems plainly to follow from God's own words to Abraham in Genesis 22 that he learns something new about the free actions of human beings.
After Abraham had shown himself ready to sacrifice his son at God's command, the Lord says: 'Now I know that you fear God, because you have not spared your only son for my sake.'

sections.title: A third objection: God 'expected' grapes and got wild grapes (Isaiah 5)
sections.pass_a: Nay Scripture seems to teach that some things happen otherwise than God himself had conjectured, since it affirms that some things are done by men, contrary to what he himself had expected. As when God thus complains of the stubbornness and rebellion of the Jewish people, What is there that I ought to have done more to my vineyard, and have not done to it? Why did I expect that it should bring forth grapes, and it brought forth wild grapes? in Isaiah chap. five.
pass_b: Scripture even seems to teach that some things turn out otherwise than God himself had supposed, since it says that people do some things contrary to what he had expected.

So God complains of the stubbornness and rebellion of the Jewish people in Isaiah 5: 'What more should I have done for my vineyard that I have not done? Why, when I expected it to yield grapes, did it yield wild grapes?'

sections.title: Reply: Scripture speaks of God's repentance figuratively; it signifies an effect, not a feeling (1 Samuel 15)
sections.pass_a: But to these it must be said, that scripture often attributes to God the members and affections of men tropically and figuratively, not however that they belong to him according to the letter and properly: and therefore many things which are said of God anthropopathos, are to be understood theoprepos, and in a manner which is worthy of God. Therefore when scripture says, that God was led by repentance, it is no more necessary that we take it properly, than that which is read elsewhere that the bowels of God were moved, and that smoke went up into his nostrils. Nay when scripture takes repentance properly, it expressly removes it from God. As when Samuel says to Saul, The Triumpher, or strength, of Israel will not lie, and will not be turned by repentance: for he is not a man that he should repent, 1 Sam. 15. Repentance therefore in God signifies not an affection, but an effect. And when scripture says God repented, it takes the antecedent for the consequent, and signifies that God did that, which a man would do who repents of a work done by himself: namely that God determined to destroy men made by himself, from the earth, on account of their iniquity; as a man destroys a work of which he repents.
pass_b: The answer is that Scripture often ascribes human limbs and feelings to God by a figure of speech, not because they belong to him literally and properly. Much that is said of God in human terms (anthropopathos) must therefore be understood in a way fitting for God (theoprepos), in a manner worthy of him.

So when Scripture says that God repented, there is no more need to take this literally than what we read elsewhere, that God's heart was stirred or that smoke rose from his nostrils. Indeed, when Scripture speaks of repentance in the proper sense, it expressly denies it of God, as when Samuel says to Saul: 'The Glory, or Strength, of Israel will not lie or change his mind, for he is not a man, that he should repent' (1 Samuel 15).

In God, then, repentance means not a feeling but an effect. When Scripture says God repented, it puts the antecedent for the consequent: it means that God did what a man does who regrets something he has made. God resolved to wipe from the earth, because of their wickedness, the human beings he had made, as a man destroys a work he regrets.

lemmas.gloss: takes the antecedent for the consequent

sections.title: God's 'sorrow' likewise puts the consequent for the antecedent
sections.pass_a: In the same way God is said to be grieved on account of the sins of men, not that he feels in himself some affection like our sadness; but simply to signify that the sins of men are much disapproved by God and displease him, and are such as would bring sadness to God, if he were like us, and homoiopathes: so that here the consequent is taken for the antecedent, sadness, namely, for that which in a capable subject is apt to beget sadness.
pass_b: In the same way God is said to be grieved by human sins, not because he feels in himself any emotion like our sadness. It is simply a way of saying that God strongly disapproves of human sins and is displeased by them, and that they are such as would bring him sorrow if he were like us and subject to the same passions.
Here the consequent is put for the antecedent: sorrow stands for what is apt to produce sorrow in a subject capable of it.

sections.title: The vineyard: God was not in doubt, but had used means from which a man could rightly hope for fruit
sections.pass_a: Similarly in Isaiah, the Lord is said to have expected grapes from his vineyard when it brought forth wild grapes; not that God was uncertain and doubtful about what the Jewish people, figured by that vineyard, would do, after so many means applied to forming it to true piety; but because he had done those things which plainly ought to bring that people back into the right way, and which, if a man had applied them towards a man, he could lawfully hope and expect that his heart would thence be softened, and bent to love and willing obedience.
pass_b: Similarly, in Isaiah the Lord is said to have expected grapes from his vineyard when it yielded wild grapes. This is not because God was uncertain or in doubt about what the Jewish people, represented by that vineyard, would do after so many means had been used to form them to true godliness.

It is because he had done what ought plainly to have brought that people back to the right path. Had one man used such means toward another, he could rightly have hoped and expected that the other's heart would be softened by them and turned to love and willing obedience.

sections.title: 'Now I know': Abraham gave certain proof of his fear of God
sections.pass_a: But when God says to Abraham, Now I know that thou fearest God, because thou hast not spared thine only begotten son for my sake. He does not mean to signify that he had before doubted of the piety of Abraham, or that Abraham had not been sufficiently known to him; but only that Abraham, while he was ready to sacrifice his own son, God commanding, gave a certain and undoubted proof of his love and fear towards God, and such by which he could be convinced, who had hitherto doubted of that matter, and had not been sufficiently certain and persuaded.
pass_b: When God says to Abraham, 'Now I know that you fear God, because you have not spared your only son for my sake,' he does not mean that he had previously doubted Abraham's godliness or had not known him well enough.

He means only that Abraham, by being ready at God's command to sacrifice his own son, gave a sure and unquestionable proof of his love and fear toward God. It was proof enough to convince anyone who had so far doubted the matter and had not been fully certain and persuaded of it.

sections.title: The objection from God's oath in Numbers 14
sections.pass_a: Nor has the argument greater force which those whom we oppose seek from the 14th chapter of the book of Numbers. Where God is said to have sworn that he would bring his people into the land of Canaan; and yet on account of their sin and unbelief he swears again that he will no more do it. As I live, says the Lord, as ye have spoken in my hearing, so will I do to you. In this wilderness shall your carcasses lie. All ye that were numbered from twenty years old and upward, and have murmured against me, ye shall not enter the land concerning which I lifted up my hand, to make you dwell therein, save Caleb the son of Jephunneh, and Joshua the son of Nun. For who, they say, among men themselves is so mad, as to swear from the heart that he will do something, which he already well knows he will by no means do, or has already most thoroughly explored causes why he will in no way do it? Or what is more unworthy of God, than to swear he will do something, not in mind, but in words only?
pass_b: The argument our opponents draw from Numbers 14 has no more force. There God is said to have sworn that he would bring his people into the land of Canaan, and yet, because of their sin and unbelief, he swears again that he will no longer do so: 'As I live, says the Lord, I will do to you just as you have spoken in my hearing. Your corpses will lie in this wilderness. None of you who were counted, from twenty years old and upward, and who grumbled against me, will enter the land I swore with raised hand to settle you in, except Caleb son of Jephunneh and Joshua son of Nun.'

'For what man,' they ask, 'is so mad as to swear in earnest that he will do something he already knows full well he will not do, or for which he already has thoroughly established reasons why he will by no means do it? And what is more unworthy of God than to swear that he will do something only in words and not in intention?'

lemmas.gloss: not in mind, but in words only

sections.title: Reply: the oath concerned the nation, or was conditional; even a good man may swear so
sections.pass_a: But it is true indeed that God often swore that he would give to the posterity of Abraham the land of Canaan, and to those oaths mentioned in many places the words which we have just cited look. But that that oath specially regarded those of the Israelites who were rebels in the desert, is not proved from the words cited, Ye shall not enter the land concerning which I lifted up my hand, to make YOU dwell therein. For there the particle You indefinitely designates the Israelite nation, not however singly the persons who then constituted it. Nor yet would there be anything absurd in it, if we said that God specially promised with an oath to those men entrance into the land of Canaan, not absolutely, but under a condition, although he foresaw that that condition would not be fulfilled by them; provided that condition pertained to their duty, and was such as they could and ought to fulfil. Nor among men themselves would he be mad, who swore to anyone that he would do this or that, provided he persisted in the duty of a good man, although he held for certain that that other would by no means perform his duty.
pass_b: It is true that God often swore to give the land of Canaan to Abraham's descendants, and the words just quoted refer to those oaths, which are recorded in many places. But the quoted words, 'You will not enter the land I swore with raised hand to settle YOU in', do not prove that the oath was aimed specifically at those Israelites who rebelled in the wilderness. There the word 'you' refers to the Israelite nation in general, not to the particular persons who made it up at the time.

Even so, there would be nothing absurd in saying that God promised those men in particular, on oath, that they would enter the land of Canaan, not absolutely but on a condition, though he foresaw that they would not meet it. All that is required is that the condition was part of their duty and was one they could and ought to fulfil.

Among human beings, too, no one would be mad who swore to someone that he would do this or that provided the other kept to the duty of a good man, even though he was sure the other would not do his duty at all.

sections.title: The Socinians' chief motive: certain foreknowledge would make God's earnest exhortations pointless
sections.pass_a: But those who today contend that there is not in God a certain foreknowledge of future contingents, are chiefly moved by this that, if God certainly foresees those things which men are going to do freely, and that from eternity, he cannot, as they think, seriously admonish, exhort, and adjure men, that they be converted and repent. For to what purpose is there need anxiously to exhort and urge someone, to do that which you hold for ascertained he will do; or for what good to use solicitation, and much adjuration, with him of whom it is explored to you that he will do none of those things which you ask?
pass_b: Those who today maintain that God has no certain foreknowledge of future contingents are moved chiefly by this. If God foresees with certainty, and from eternity, what human beings will freely do, then in their view he cannot seriously warn, exhort and implore them to turn and repent.

'What need is there,' they ask, 'to exhort and press someone earnestly to do what you know for sure he will do? And what is the good of much pleading and imploring with someone who, as you well know, will do none of the things you ask?'

choices.why: The Schools' term for future events without a necessary and determinate cause; kept as a technical term.

sections.title: Reply: God foresees obedience or defiance only as following his earnest warnings, which are means to obedience
sections.pass_a: But so far is it from being the case that the foreseen stubbornness, or obedience of men hinders God from being able seriously to admonish, ask, and exhort them: that on the contrary God cannot foresee it, without first foreseeing, and determining with himself that he will deal thus seriously with men. For divine admonitions, exhortations, and adjurations are means by which the obedience of men is procured; and certain presuppositions, without which they cannot be and be called rebels to God, and stubborn against him.
pass_b: Far from preventing God from earnestly warning, asking and exhorting human beings, their foreseen defiance or obedience is something God cannot foresee without first foreseeing, and resolving within himself, that he will deal with them earnestly in this way.

God's warnings, exhortations and pleas are the means by which human obedience is brought about. They are also presupposed conditions without which people cannot be, or be called, rebels against God and defiant toward him.

sections.title: Even the Socinians grant that God pleads with the hardened, as with Pharaoh
sections.pass_a: But that it does not misbecome the divine wisdom, that those whom God certainly knows will by no means obey his admonitions, exhortations, and precepts, he nevertheless urges, exhorts and invites by all means to repentance, those very persons with whom we have to do can be convinced. For they confess that some, the divine judgment avenging their obstinate malice, are so blinded and hardened, that they cannot repent. And yet they cannot deny that God towards those very persons whom he very well knows to be so affected and disposed, uses the admonitions, and adjurations by which he is wont to urge men to duty, as is manifest even from the single example of Pharaoh. If therefore in these, or about these, our adversaries confessing it, serious adjurations, threatenings, complaints of God can have place, without any violation of the justice of God, or diminution of his wisdom, why should not the same be able to have place in the rest, whom God from eternity, from the free purpose of their will and mind, knew would not obey?
pass_b: Our opponents themselves can be convinced that it is not unworthy of God's wisdom to urge, exhort and invite to repentance, by every means, those he knows for certain will never obey his warnings, exhortations and commands. They admit that some, by God's judgment punishing their stubborn wickedness, are so blinded and hardened that they cannot repent.

Yet they cannot deny that toward those very people, whom he knows perfectly well to be in that state, God uses the warnings and pleas by which he ordinarily calls human beings to their duty, as the example of Pharaoh alone makes plain.

If, then, by our opponents' own admission, God's earnest pleas, threats and complaints can have a place with such people, without any breach of his justice or loss to his wisdom, why can the same not hold for all the others whom God knew from eternity would not obey, out of the free purpose of their own will and mind?

sections.title: The objections from Scripture fail; the real difficulty: foreknowledge seems to make every event necessary
sections.pass_a: Vain therefore are whatever things are brought forward from the scriptures against the eternal foreknowledge of God, by which he knows certainly and distinctly whatever things are to be done freely by creatures at any time. It follows now that we see how the liberty of creatures in acting can stand with that eternal foreknowledge of God. For there is here no little difficulty which has long exercised the wits of the Doctors. For since it is impossible that the foreknowledge of God be deceived, it cannot be that those things should not come to pass which God foresaw would come to pass; and so all things come to pass necessarily, and it is impossible that the very will of men should not produce and elicit those acts, which God foreknows from eternity are to be produced by it: and so the liberty of human actions seems to perish altogether. For by what reason can that be called free, which it is impossible should not be done, or be done otherwise?
pass_b: All the arguments drawn from Scripture against God's eternal foreknowledge, by which he knows certainly and distinctly whatever creatures will freely do at any time, are therefore empty.

We must now consider how the freedom of creatures in acting can coexist with that eternal foreknowledge of God. There is no small difficulty here, one that has long exercised the minds of learned teachers. Since God's foreknowledge cannot be mistaken, what God foresaw would happen cannot fail to happen. So everything happens necessarily, and the human will cannot fail to produce and elicit the acts God foreknows from eternity that it will produce. In that case the freedom of human actions seems to vanish entirely. For how can something be called free if it is impossible for it not to happen, or to happen otherwise?
